body:
What Makes a Shape?: 1. 3. 2. No; a shape's name comes from its sides and corners, not its color. 3. No; its sides are not all the same length (it is a rectangle). 4. Any closed shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners; yes, it is still a triangle.
Build New Shapes: the drawing shows two or more smaller shapes put together with their edges touching, and the student names the shapes used and the new shape (for example, two triangles make a square; two squares make a rectangle; four quarter-circles make a circle).
Halves and Fourths: 1. A circle split by one line through the middle into 2 equal shares; each share is a half. 2. A rectangle split into 4 equal shares; each share is a fourth (or a quarter). 3. No; halves must be 2 equal shares, and these parts are not the same size. 4. One fourth (a quarter) of the pizza. 5. One half; when you cut the same pizza into more equal shares, each share is smaller.
Shapes and Shares Check: 1. 4 sides and 4 corners. 2. A triangle. 3. Any two shapes that make a rectangle, such as two squares, two smaller rectangles or two triangles. 4. A square split into 2 equal shares (one straight line across the middle, up and down, side to side or corner to corner). 5. A circle split into 4 equal shares with one share colored. 6. One half; fewer equal shares means bigger shares.
Scoring tip: shares only need to look about equal in a first grader's drawing; score the idea of equal shares, not ruler-straight lines. A student who says a fourth is bigger "because 4 is more than 2" is Not yet on problem 6; fold two paper circles to show it.
title: Answer key: Shapes and Equal Shares
